name: Kailasanathar Temple, Rajapathy
deity: Shiva as Kailasanathar, with the Goddess Soundara Nayaki
period: Eighth of the Nava Kailasam, the shrine of Ketu; a village temple of the lower Tamiraparani
summary: In the village of Rajapathy near Kurumbur, where the Tamiraparani nears the sea, Shiva as Kailasanathar keeps the eighth of the Nava Kailasam — the shrine of Ketu, the shadow planet.

sections.history: Rajapathy is a small village in the Tiruchendur block of Thoothukudi district, on the lower course of the Tamiraparani, a few kilometres from Kurumbur on the road to Tiruchendur. Its Kailasanathar temple is the eighth of the Nava Kailasam and the shrine of Ketu, the southern node of the moon. Unlike some of its sister shrines upstream, the temple has no well-known inscriptions to fix its age, and it is remembered above all through the circuit to which it belongs. It remains a living village temple, cared for by its community and kept freshly painted, and its standing comes from its place in the river's chain of nine.
sections.architecture: The temple is a modest Dravidian shrine with its sanctum, a Nandi facing the lord, and a separate shrine for the Goddess Soundara Nayaki. Its most striking feature is in the sanctum itself: the linga is shown with four wheels, as though the lord rides in a chariot. A separate Navagraha shrine departs from the usual images of the nine planets — here every graha is represented by a Shiva linga, a reminder that Shiva is held to be the master of all the planets.
sections.legends: In the Nava Kailasam story, the eighth of the lotuses set afloat on the Tamiraparani by Romasa, the disciple of Agastya, came to rest at Rajapathy, and a linga was consecrated where it stopped. Tradition holds that Ketu himself worshipped Shiva here to be freed of his own afflictions, which is why the shrine is sought by those troubled by Ketu in their horoscopes, and why it is sometimes spoken of as a southern Kalahasti, after the great Rahu–Ketu shrine of Andhra. Besides the river, the temple counts the Palazhi theertham among its sacred waters.
sections.festivals: Special worship for relief from the effects of Ketu is customarily offered on Sundays and Tuesdays, and those passing through the seven-year period of Rahu also come to pray. Maha Shivaratri and the monthly pradosham are kept as at every Shiva temple. Confirm dates locally.
sections.experience: Rajapathy is the quietest of the downstream shrines, reached by village roads from Kurumbur. Pilgrims come with a particular purpose — a remedy for Ketu — and linger before the chariot-wheeled linga and the unusual Navagraha shrine of nine lingas before continuing to the last of the circuit, Senthapoomangalam, near the river mouth.

visit.timings: Open daily with morning and evening darshan sessions and a midday closure; Sundays and Tuesdays draw the most devotees. Confirm current timings locally before visiting.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — shoulders and knees covered; footwear removed before entering. Men are traditionally asked to remove the upper garment before the sanctum, as at many southern shrines; follow the posted rules.
visit.photography: Photography is restricted in and around the sanctum; follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.gettingThere: Rajapathy lies in Thoothukudi district near Kurumbur, about 45 km from Tirunelveli on the road to Tiruchendur and roughly 32 km from Thoothukudi. Kurumbur, on the Tirunelveli–Tiruchendur railway line, is the nearest station, with local minibuses to the village; Thoothukudi is the nearest airport.
